stem: The value of \(\left\lbrack \text{H}^{+} \right\rbrack\) in \(\text{mol L}^{- 1}\) of \(0.001\text{ M}\) acetic acid solution \(\left( K_{\text{a}} = 1.8 \times 10^{- 5} \right)\) is ______.
solution:
**(B)** \(1.34 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}\)

Acetic acid is a weak acid and ionises only partially :

\(\mathrm{CH_3COOH(aq)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3COO^{\ominus}(aq)} + \mathrm{H^{\oplus}(aq)}\)

Let \(\alpha\) be its degree of dissociation in a solution of concentration \(c\). Of the \(c\) mol dm\(^{-3}\) taken, \(\alpha c\) dissociates, so at equilibrium

\([\mathrm{H^{\oplus}}] = [\mathrm{CH_3COO^{\ominus}}] = \alpha c\) and \([\mathrm{CH_3COOH}] = c - \alpha c = c(1 - \alpha)\)

Hence the dissociation constant is

\(K_a = \frac{[\mathrm{CH_3COO^{\ominus}}][\mathrm{H^{\oplus}}]}{[\mathrm{CH_3COOH}]} = \frac{\alpha c \times \alpha c}{c(1 - \alpha)} = \frac{\alpha^2 c}{1 - \alpha}\)

A weak acid is slightly dissociated, so \((1 - \alpha) \approx 1\) and \(K_a = \alpha^2 c\). This gives

\(\alpha = \sqrt{\frac{K_a}{c}}\), so \([\mathrm{H^{\oplus}}] = \alpha c = \sqrt{K_a c}\)

Substituting \(K_a = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}\) and \(c = 0.001\ \mathrm{M} = 1 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{M}\),

\([\mathrm{H^{\oplus}}] = \sqrt{1.8 \times 10^{-5} \times 1 \times 10^{-3}} = \sqrt{1.8 \times 10^{-8}} = \sqrt{1.8} \times 10^{-4}\)

\(\therefore\ [\mathrm{H^{\oplus}}] = 1.34 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}\)

Check : a monobasic acid cannot furnish more \(\mathrm{H^{\oplus}}\) than the acid taken, so \([\mathrm{H^{\oplus}}]\) must lie below \(1 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{M}\). The values \(1.34 \times 10^{-3}\), \(1.34 \times 10^{-2}\) and \(1.34 \times 10^{-1}\) are respectively \(1.34\), \(13.4\) and \(134\) times the acid taken, so no solution of this acid can reach any of them. The value \(1.34 \times 10^{-4}\) is \(13.4\%\) of the acid taken, a partial ionisation as a weak acid requires. Keeping the \((1 - \alpha)\) term instead of dropping it means solving \(x^2 + K_a x - K_a c = 0\), whose positive root is \(1.25 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}\) : the same power of ten, so the choice does not change.

stem: The \(\text{pH}\) of weak monoacidic base is \(11.2\), its \(\text{OH}^{-}\) ion concentration is:
solution:
**(A)** \(1.585 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\)

For any aqueous solution at 298 K the ionic product of water gives \(\mathrm{pH} + \mathrm{pOH} = 14\). The solution has \(\mathrm{pH} = 11.2\), so

\(\mathrm{pOH} = 14 - \mathrm{pH} = 14 - 11.2 = 2.8\)

By definition \(\mathrm{pOH} = -\log_{10}[\mathrm{OH^{\ominus}}]\), hence

\(\log_{10}[\mathrm{OH^{\ominus}}] = -\mathrm{pOH} = -2.8 = -3 + 0.2 = \bar{3}.2\)

\([\mathrm{OH^{\ominus}}] = \mathrm{antilog}\ \bar{3}.2\)

\(\therefore\ [\mathrm{OH^{\ominus}}] = 1.585 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\)

Check by working each printed value back to a pH. \(1.585 \times 10^{-3}\) gives \(\mathrm{pOH} = 3 - 0.200 = 2.8\) and \(\mathrm{pH} = 11.2\), the value stated in the question. \(3.010 \times 10^{-3}\) gives \(\mathrm{pOH} = 3 - 0.479 = 2.52\) and \(\mathrm{pH} = 11.48\), which is not \(11.2\). \(1.585 \times 10^{-11}\) gives \(\mathrm{pOH} = 11 - 0.200 = 10.8\) and \(\mathrm{pH} = 3.2\), and \(3.010 \times 10^{-11}\) gives \(\mathrm{pOH} = 10.52\) and \(\mathrm{pH} = 3.48\) : both describe an acidic solution, which a solution of a base cannot be. A base has \(\mathrm{pH} > 7\), so its \([\mathrm{OH^{\ominus}}]\) must exceed the neutral \(1 \times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\), and only the two values at \(10^{-3}\) do.

stem: The \(\text{pH}\) of \(0.001\text{ M HCl}\) solution is ______.
solution:
**(B)** \(3\)

\(\mathrm{HCl}\) is a strong acid and is almost completely dissociated in water :

\(\mathrm{HCl(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2O}(l) \longrightarrow \mathrm{H_3O^{\oplus}(aq)} + \mathrm{Cl^{\ominus}(aq)}\)

It is monobasic, so one mole of \(\mathrm{HCl}\) furnishes one mole of \(\mathrm{H_3O^{\oplus}}\) and the hydronium ion concentration equals the concentration of the acid taken :

\([\mathrm{H_3O^{\oplus}}] = c = 0.001\ \mathrm{M} = 1 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{M}\)

\(\mathrm{pH} = -\log_{10}[\mathrm{H_3O^{\oplus}}] = -\log_{10}(1 \times 10^{-3}) = -(-3)\)

\(\therefore\ \mathrm{pH} = 3\)

Check : \(\mathrm{pH} = 3\) returns \([\mathrm{H_3O^{\oplus}}] = 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{M}\), the concentration that was taken. Of the other printed values, \(2\) would require \(0.01\ \mathrm{M}\) acid, ten times the concentration given, while \(10\) and \(11\) both lie above \(7\) and so describe a basic solution, which a solution of a strong acid cannot be.

stem: Which formula co-relates degree of dissociation (\(\alpha\)) and concentration (\(c\)) of electrolyte?
solution:
**(B)** \(\alpha = \sqrt{\frac{K_a}{c}}\)

Consider a weak electrolyte \(\mathrm{AB}\) of concentration \(c\) ionising as

\(\mathrm{AB(aq)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{A^{\oplus}(aq)} + \mathrm{B^{\ominus}(aq)}\)

and let \(\alpha\) be its degree of dissociation at equilibrium. Of the \(c\) mol dm\(^{-3}\) taken, \(\alpha c\) dissociates, so

\([\mathrm{A^{\oplus}}] = [\mathrm{B^{\ominus}}] = \alpha c\) and \([\mathrm{AB}] = c - \alpha c = c(1 - \alpha)\)

The dissociation constant is therefore

\(K_a = \frac{[\mathrm{A^{\oplus}}][\mathrm{B^{\ominus}}]}{[\mathrm{AB}]} = \frac{\alpha c \times \alpha c}{c(1 - \alpha)} = \frac{\alpha^2 c}{1 - \alpha}\)

which is Ostwald's dilution law. A weak electrolyte is only slightly dissociated, so \(\alpha \ll 1\) and \((1 - \alpha) \approx 1\), leaving

\(K_a = \alpha^2 c\), that is \(\alpha^2 = \frac{K_a}{c}\)

\(\therefore\ \alpha = \sqrt{\frac{K_a}{c}}\)

Check by squaring each printed relation and seeing which returns \(K_a = \alpha^2 c\). Squaring \(\alpha = \sqrt{K_a/c}\) gives \(\alpha^2 = K_a/c\), that is \(K_a = \alpha^2 c\), the law just derived. Squaring \(c = \sqrt{K_a/\alpha}\) gives \(c^2 = K_a/\alpha\), that is \(K_a = \alpha c^2\); squaring \(c = \sqrt{K_a \alpha}\) gives \(K_a = c^2/\alpha\); and squaring \(c = \sqrt{\alpha/K_a}\) gives \(K_a = \alpha/c^2\). None of those three is Ostwald's law, and each makes the wrong quantity the subject, since the question asks for \(\alpha\). A numerical test of the accepted relation : for \(K_a = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}\) in \(0.01\ \mathrm{M}\) solution it gives \(\alpha = \sqrt{1.8 \times 10^{-3}} = 4.24 \times 10^{-2}\), and substituting back, \(\alpha^2 c = (4.24 \times 10^{-2})^2 \times 1 \times 10^{-2} = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}\), which is \(K_a\).

stem: The formula used to calculate molar conductivity of an electrolyte is ______.
solution:
**(C)** \(\Lambda = \frac{1000k}{c}\)

Molar conductivity is the conducting power of ALL the ions furnished by one mole of the electrolyte, that is the conductivity of a solution containing one mole of it :

\(\Lambda = \frac{k}{C}\)

Here \(k\) is the conductivity of the solution, in \(\mathrm{S\ cm^{-1}}\), and \(C\) is the concentration expressed in \(\mathrm{mol\ cm^{-3}}\).

Concentration is measured in \(\mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\), and \(1\ \mathrm{dm^3} = 1000\ \mathrm{cm^3}\), so a solution of \(c\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\) holds

\(C = \frac{c}{1000}\ \mathrm{mol\ cm^{-3}}\)

Substituting this in \(\Lambda = k/C\),

\(\Lambda = \frac{k}{\left( \frac{c}{1000} \right)}\)

\(\therefore\ \Lambda = \frac{1000k}{c}\)

Check the units : \(\mathrm{S\ cm^{-1}} \div \mathrm{mol\ cm^{-3}} = \mathrm{S\ cm^{2}\ mol^{-1}}\), which is the unit of molar conductivity. Testing the other printed relations : \(\Lambda = 1000c/k\) interchanges \(k\) and \(c\), so it would make the molar conductivity fall as the solution conducts better, and its units are \(\mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\) divided by \(\mathrm{S\ cm^{-1}}\), which is not \(\mathrm{S\ cm^{2}\ mol^{-1}}\). \(C = 1000\Lambda/k\) rearranges to \(\Lambda = kc/1000\), which would drive \(\Lambda\) to zero on dilution instead of raising it towards its limiting value \(\Lambda_0\). \(k = 1000/(\Lambda c)\) makes the conductivity rise without limit as \(c\) falls, whereas a solution holding no electrolyte conducts no current at all.
